newsitem.title: CROATIA: Moslem-Croat relations in Bosnia worsen-ministers.
newsitem.headline: Moslem-Croat relations in Bosnia worsen-ministers.

text.p: Relations between Moslem and Croat partners in Bosnia's federation have worsened and a high-level meeting is needed to repair the damage, the foreign ministers of Croatia and Bosnia said on Friday.

Mate Granic of Croatia and Jadranko Prlic, a Croat minister in the mixed Moslem-Croat Bosnian federation government, met in Zagreb to discuss problems burdening the uneasy alliance, the state news agency Hina reported.
"Relations between Croats and Bosniaks (Moslems) have lately ...artificially worsened," Prlic was quoted as saying by Hina.

Granic said: "In view of certain problems in the functioning of and the cooperation within Bosnia, particularly between Croats and Moslems, our joint position is that a meeting of the Federation Forum should be set up as soon as possible."
He was referring to a body, set up by the United States in 1995, to deal with any outstanding problems between Moslems and Croats should they threaten the federation.
Under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement on Bosnia, the Moslem-Croat federation controls just over half of the country and a Serb entity the rest.

Moslems and Croats started as allies when fighting broke out against Serbs in 1992 after Bosnia's declaration of independence from Yugoslavia but they fell out the next year in a bloody sideshow war in central and southern Bosnia.

A U.S. diplomatic initiative brought them back together in early 1994 but the federation has never worked smoothly. Ethnically-motivated incidents in the southern town of Mostar in the past few weeks have heightened tensions.

The federal parliament convened on Wednesday without Croat deputies after the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) told its officials in federal bodies to freeze their mandates pending a proper power-sharing agreement with Moslems.
The HDZ said the next federal president should be a Croat and Croats should get six ministerial postn and Croatian officials to meet soon to resolve open questions.
Croatia has supported nationalist Croats in Bosnia, financing their efforts to carve out a separate state which have severely weakened the federation from the start.
"There are no open issues which could not be resolved in a concrete political dialogue," Prlic said.
He was not accompanied with any of the Moslem officials from his ministry and the Bosnian ambassador to Zagreb, Kasim Trnka, also failed to show up.
Asked if this meant that he came to Zagreb without the consent or knowledge of his Moslem partners, Prlic said the trip was arranged a week ago and both Moslems and Serbs knew about it.
